passages.title: The Fireflies and the Crossing
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Each night, three fireflies guided small animals across a reed bed. One blinked twice near the entrance. Another flashed in circles above the safe stones. The third shone without stopping beside the far bank. For years, travelers followed this pattern easily.

Then each firefly decided that its own signal deserved more attention. All three began blinking as fast as they could. A young snail entered the reeds, saw light everywhere, and turned back. The fireflies had made the path brighter but the directions weaker.

They tried again. The first marked the entrance and then went dark. The second flashed only above the next safe stone. The third waited until the traveler reached the far bank. This time, the snail crossed without a wrong turn.

The fireflies kept their separate tasks after that night. None made the whole journey visible alone. Together, their lights formed a clear sequence. A signal becomes useful when others know what part of the path it marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the fable’s main idea?
choices: Distinct signals work together when each one clearly marks its own part of a shared route.
The brightest possible path always gives travelers the clearest directions.
A traveler should wait until one guide can light an entire journey alone.
Fireflies can guide others only by shining without stopping.
questions.explanation: The failed crossing has competing lights, while the successful crossing gives each firefly one clear place in the sequence.

questions.stem: Why did more light make the directions weaker?
choices: The snail could not see any of the fireflies in the reeds.
The competing flashes no longer showed which light marked each step of the route.
The far bank moved whenever all three fireflies blinked.
The safe stones disappeared because the night became too bright.
questions.explanation: When every firefly flashed rapidly, light appeared everywhere and the snail could not read the former pattern.

questions.stem: What does “sequence” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a light that never changes
a path hidden beneath deep water
a set of signals arranged in a useful order
a contest to produce the brightest flash
questions.explanation: The entrance, safe stone, and far bank signals guide the snail one after another, forming an ordered series.

questions.stem: What task did the third firefly take during the successful crossing?
choices: It circled above every safe stone.
It followed the snail into the reeds.
It marked the entrance and then went dark.
It waited beside the far bank until the traveler arrived.
questions.explanation: During the second attempt, the third firefly waits until the traveler reaches the far bank.

lesson.strategy: Track the same three guides across two crossings. Compare their competing flashes with their later division of tasks, then connect the snail’s outcomes to the moral.

signals.means: This introduces the selfish change that disrupts the familiar guidance pattern.
The fable begins its corrective attempt after the snail turns back.
These words mark the successful result of restoring distinct roles.

vocab.inContext: the familiar arrangement of three different guiding lights
signals presented in an order that matches the route
a light used to communicate where a traveler should look

skillTips.main-idea: State what changes between the failed and successful crossings: separate tasks replace a contest for attention.
skillTips.inference: Infer the snail’s confusion from “light everywhere” and the loss of each signal’s clear location.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the ordered places (entrance, stone, and far bank) to determine the contextual meaning of “sequence.”
skillTips.detail: Match each firefly to one location during the second attempt before choosing the third firefly’s task.

passages.title: What a Promise Changes
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When Lila promises to unlock the workshop at eight, her sentence changes other people’s plans. One neighbor agrees to bring wood. Another delays an errand so the tools will not be left alone. A prediction about the weather may guide action too, but a promise does something more: it gives the speaker a responsibility for what others reasonably rely on.

Does the responsibility come only from the words? A person may repeat a promise without understanding it, or may be forced to speak. In such cases, the sentence sounds complete while the commitment is damaged. Intention matters. So do the shared practices that let listeners recognize what has been offered.

Circumstances can change after a sincere promise. If a burst pipe closes the workshop, Lila cannot unlock it safely. Keeping the literal schedule would defeat the purpose that everyone expected. She still owes the others an explanation, a warning, and help making a new plan.

A promise therefore reaches beyond private intention without becoming an unbreakable command. It creates a social bond through words, reliance, and accepted rules. When fulfillment becomes impossible, responsibility may shift from doing exactly what was said to repairing the coordination that the promise made possible.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage’s main idea?
choices: A promise is merely a prediction that later events will probably occur.
A promise creates responsibility through intention, shared rules, and others’ reliance, even when changed circumstances require repair instead of literal fulfillment.
Every sincere promise must be completed exactly as stated, regardless of danger.
Words create a commitment even when a speaker is forced to repeat them without understanding.
questions.explanation: The passage joins intention, recognizable social practice, and reliance, then shows how responsibility can shift when fulfillment becomes unsafe.

questions.stem: Why would Lila still owe others a warning if the burst pipe prevents her from opening the workshop?
choices: The warning would make the burst pipe disappear before eight.
A warning would prove that the workshop never needed to open.
Other people changed their plans in reasonable reliance on her commitment.
The promise required her to keep all information private.
questions.explanation: The opening shows neighbors arranging work and errands around Lila’s promise, so they need new information when the plan fails.

questions.stem: What does “literal” mean in the phrase “Keeping the literal schedule”?
choices: hidden from everyone except the speaker
revised by a group after a long debate
based only on what might happen later
followed exactly according to the stated words
questions.explanation: The contrast is between opening exactly at eight as stated and changing the action because the burst pipe makes that unsafe.

questions.stem: What changed circumstance prevents Lila from safely keeping the original schedule?
choices: A burst pipe closes the workshop.
The neighbors bring the wrong kind of wood.
The tools have already been moved elsewhere.
A weather prediction changes during the night.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph specifically says a burst pipe closes the workshop and makes unlocking it unsafe.

lesson.strategy: Separate a promise from a prediction, then test responsibility in three conditions: sincere reliance, forced words, and a later obstacle that makes exact performance unsafe.

signals.phrase: but a promise does something more
signals.means: This contrast introduces the added responsibility that distinguishes promising from predicting.
The phrase applies the argument to words spoken without understanding or free intention.
The conclusion combines private intention with the social effects of a commitment.

vocab.inContext: a responsibility the speaker intentionally undertakes
other people organizing their actions around the promise
carrying out what the promise originally required

skillTips.main-idea: Include both how a promise gains force and how responsibility changes when exact fulfillment becomes impossible.
skillTips.inference: Use the neighbors’ altered plans as evidence that Lila must repair coordination even though the pipe is not her fault.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast the exact eight o’clock schedule with the safer changed plan to interpret “literal” in context.
skillTips.detail: Find the concrete obstacle in the third paragraph rather than choosing the earlier weather prediction example.

passages.title: How Shared Labels Take Shape
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Two volunteers are sorting unfamiliar hardware during a phone call. One describes a metal piece as the bent silver strip with two holes. After the other finds it and confirms the match, both begin using elbow as its short name. A long description has become a short shared label.

Psychologists study this kind of coordination by giving pairs unusual shapes or objects that lack familiar names. Early descriptions are often detailed because speakers cannot assume which feature a partner will notice. Listeners respond with questions, corrections, or signs of understanding. Through this exchange, the pair builds common ground: information each person has reason to treat as shared.

On later rounds, the same partners can use shorter expressions. The efficiency belongs to the pair, however, not automatically to everyone who knows the language. A newcomer hearing elbow may imagine a bent arm rather than a small metal strip. The experienced speaker must expand the label again or explain its local history.

Conversation, then, is not simply a package sent from one mind to another. Speakers propose descriptions, listeners test them, and both repair failures. Even a quick confirmation does work: it helps turn a private guess into a usable reference. Shared labels save effort because earlier cooperation remains available inside later words.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Speakers communicate most efficiently by inventing private labels before meeting a partner.
A familiar word always creates the same mental picture for every listener.
Conversation partners build efficient shared labels through confirmation and repair, but those labels may not work for newcomers.
Long descriptions prevent people from reaching common ground about unfamiliar objects.
questions.explanation: The passage traces a label from detailed description to efficient shorthand, then shows why a newcomer may lack the pair’s shared history.

questions.stem: Why might the experienced speaker need to expand the label for a newcomer?
choices: Newcomers are unable to understand any short word.
The hardware changes shape whenever a new person joins.
The original partners have forgotten the first description.
The newcomer did not participate in the exchanges that gave the short label its local meaning.
questions.explanation: The efficiency belongs to the original pair because their earlier confirmation established what elbow referred to in that task.

questions.stem: What does “local” mean in the phrase “its local history”?
choices: specific to the pair and their shared situation
stored in a place close to the hardware
spoken only by people from one city
limited to objects that have familiar names
questions.explanation: The label’s history was created by these partners during their task, so local means particular to their shared interaction.

questions.stem: How can listeners respond while a pair builds common ground?
choices: By silently replacing every unfamiliar object
With questions, corrections, or signs of understanding
By refusing to use any description more than once
With a list of labels created by a different pair
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly lists questions, corrections, and signs of understanding as listener responses.

lesson.strategy: Follow one reference from full description to the shorter name elbow, then test its limits with the newcomer. Notice how listener feedback makes the shortcut possible.

signals.means: Confirmation establishes that both volunteers have matched the same object.
This time marker introduces the shorter language made possible by earlier work.
The contrast limits the label’s efficiency to people who share its history.

vocab.inContext: the partners adjusting their language and understanding together
information both partners have reason to treat as shared
a word or description used to identify a particular object

skillTips.main-idea: State both the efficiency gained by the original pair and the reason their shortcut may fail with a newcomer.
skillTips.inference: Ask what information the newcomer missed: the earlier description, confirmation, and repeated use that established elbow.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read “local” against the contrast between the experienced pair and everyone else who speaks the language.
skillTips.detail: The second paragraph names three listener responses; retrieve that list rather than inventing another form of feedback.

passages.title: How Version Control Protects Shared Work
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A neighborhood team keeps an evacuation map in a shared digital project. Mira adds the location of a new gate while Chen corrects the name of a road. Both begin from revision 12, work separately, and submit a proposed revision 13. If the system stored only the newest complete file, one person’s useful change could overwrite the other.

Version control instead records a history of changes. It can compare each proposal with the common ancestor, revision 12. Because the gate and road name affect different parts of the map, the system may merge them automatically into one new version. The history still records who changed what and which earlier state came before it.

A harder case appears when both volunteers edit the same route note in different ways. The software can mark a conflict, but it cannot know whether the route is closed, renamed, or merely described differently. A person must inspect both proposals, check the real situation, and choose or write the final wording. After that decision, the resolved version joins the history.

Branches let a team test changes without immediately altering the agreed copy. They support parallel work, not parallel truth. The repository remains useful only when people describe revisions clearly, review important merges, and keep its shared version connected to reality. Version control protects collaboration by preserving differences and making collisions visible; it does not remove the need for judgment.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the passage’s main idea?
choices: Version control guarantees that every proposed map change matches the real world.
The newest complete file is always the safest way to combine two people’s work.
Branches eliminate the need for people to review changes that affect the same route.
Version control preserves parallel changes and exposes conflicts so teams can combine work without giving up human judgment.
questions.explanation: The system merges nonoverlapping work and marks collisions, while people still must resolve disputed wording and verify reality.

questions.stem: Why must a person resolve two different edits to the same route note?
choices: The software can detect overlap but lacks enough real-world context to decide which description is true.
The software immediately deletes both edits whenever they mention one route.
A shared project cannot preserve more than one proposed revision.
People are required to reject every change created on a branch.
questions.explanation: The passage says software can mark the conflict but cannot determine whether the route is closed, renamed, or differently described.

questions.stem: What does “common ancestor” mean in this example?
choices: the volunteer who created the first neighborhood map
the earlier revision from which both proposed changes began
the final version chosen after a conflict is resolved
a separate branch that contains no project history
questions.explanation: Both volunteers start from revision 12, which the system uses as the shared earlier state for comparing their proposals.

questions.stem: Why may the gate addition and road-name correction merge automatically?
choices: They were submitted by the same volunteer.
They both replace all of revision 12.
They affect different parts of the map.
They describe the same route note differently.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the two changes touch different parts, allowing the system to combine them without a conflict.

lesson.strategy: Use revision 12 as the shared starting point. Compare the easy merge with the same-note conflict, then read branches and history as supports for review rather than substitutes for it.

signals.means: This introduces history-based tracking as the answer to accidental overwriting.
The passage moves from nonoverlapping edits to a conflict requiring judgment.
The human resolution becomes the next recorded state in the project’s history.

vocab.inContext: combine compatible changes into one new project version
overlapping edits that the system cannot safely reconcile alone
the shared project store that keeps files and their change history

skillTips.main-idea: Balance the tool’s protection against overwriting with the passage’s repeated limit: people still judge truth and importance.
skillTips.inference: Distinguish detecting two edits from knowing the real route; only the latter can settle which wording belongs on the map.
skillTips.vocabulary: Trace both proposals backward to revision 12 to see why that earlier state is their “common ancestor.”
skillTips.detail: The automatic merge depends on location: the gate and road name change separate parts of the shared map.

passages.title: The Baskets at Dawn
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At dawn, seven baskets waited beside the river ferry. Rain had blurred every paper label. Niko had to place each basket on the right village dock before the market opened.

He noticed different knots in the handle cords. Two baskets had one knot, three had two knots, and the last pair had three. The ferry pilot remembered that the docks also used one, two, or three white posts. Together, they matched the baskets to the stops.

Niko wrote the knot code on a dry board inside the cabin. At each dock, he checked the cord and the posts before unloading. Every basket reached its owner. The next morning, sellers brought wooden tags instead of paper ones. Niko kept the board anyway. A small record could help the next crew when rain returned.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the story’s main idea?
choices: Niko and the ferry pilot use matching knots and dock posts to deliver blurred-label baskets, then preserve the code for others.
Niko delays every basket until the sellers can replace its paper label.
The ferry pilot removes the white posts because they confuse the market sellers.
Wooden tags fail in the rain, so the crew returns to paper labels.
questions.explanation: The story’s problem, solution, and lasting outcome are the ruined labels, the matched code, and the saved board.

questions.stem: Why does Niko keep the code board after sellers bring wooden tags?
choices: He plans to hide the dock posts from the next crew.
The record may help future workers solve the same problem without relying on memory.
He wants every seller to stop using knots on basket cords.
The wooden tags have already blurred inside the dry cabin.
questions.explanation: The final sentence says the small record could help the next crew when rain returned, showing its value beyond that morning.

questions.stem: What does “blurred” mean in the story?
choices: tied together with matching knots
moved to the wrong village dock
made unclear and difficult to read
protected by a smooth wooden cover
questions.explanation: Rain damaged every paper label, creating the delivery problem because the writing could no longer guide the crew.

questions.stem: How many knots did the last pair of baskets have?
choices: No knots
One knot
Two knots
Three knots
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that the last pair of baskets had three knots.

lesson.strategy: Follow Niko from unreadable labels to two matching clues: cord knots and dock posts. Then notice how the dry board turns one solution into help for a later crew.

signals.means: Niko discovers the first clue that can replace the ruined labels.
Niko’s clue and the pilot’s memory combine into a usable route code.
This time shift reveals both the sellers’ change and Niko’s lasting record.

vocab.inContext: made too unclear by rain for the crew to read
strong strings forming the basket handles
taking a basket off the ferry at its stop

skillTips.main-idea: Include the delivery problem, the two-part code, and the choice to preserve the solution for later crews.
skillTips.inference: The board remains useful because written shared knowledge can outlast one worker’s memory and one dry morning.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the rain-damaged paper labels and the need for another code to infer what “blurred” did to the writing.
skillTips.detail: Read the basket groups in order: two with one knot, three with two, and the last pair with three.

passages.title: Messages Across the Semaphore Towers
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before electric wires carried news, France built chains of signal towers. In 1792, Claude Chappe demonstrated an optical telegraph. A tall mechanism on each tower had moving arms that operators could place in many positions. Each position stood for a number connected to a coded word or phrase.

An operator watched the previous tower through a telescope. When its arms changed, the operator copied the position for the next tower to see. In this way, a message moved across the landscape without one messenger traveling the whole route. The network later linked Paris with distant cities and served the government.

The system was fast for its era, but visibility set a firm limit. Fog, heavy rain, darkness, or a blocked view could stop the relay. Towers also needed trained operators and an agreed code. Chappe’s network joined mechanics, language, and a line of attentive people. Its moving arms carried information only because every station performed the same small act in order.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: France’s signal towers worked in all weather without trained operators.
Chappe’s optical telegraph relayed coded arm positions across connected towers, sending messages quickly for its era but depending on visibility and coordinated operators.
Electric wires powered the moving arms on every French semaphore tower in 1792.
One messenger carried each coded phrase from Paris along the full route.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the tower-to-tower relay and shared code, then identifies poor visibility as the system’s main limit.

questions.stem: Why did an operator use a telescope?
choices: To read messages carried on electric wires below the tower
To study the weather after darkness had stopped the relay
To see the arm positions displayed by the neighboring tower across a distance
To choose a different code without informing the next station
questions.explanation: Operators had to observe and copy the previous tower’s arm position, so the telescope made that distant visual signal readable.

questions.stem: In this passage, what does “relay” mean?
choices: a machine powered by an underground wire
a single journey made by one messenger
a book that lists every government phrase
the passing of a signal from one station to the next
questions.explanation: Each operator copies the previous tower for the next one, so relay means repeated passing along the chain.

questions.stem: In what year did Claude Chappe demonstrate the optical telegraph?
questions.explanation: The first paragraph directly dates Chappe’s demonstration to 1792.

lesson.strategy: Trace one arm position through the relay: display, telescope, copy, and repeat. Then set the network’s speed beside its dependence on clear sight and trained people.

signals.means: The phrase turns the repeated copying process into movement across the landscape.
This contrast introduces the optical network’s central operating limit.
The conclusion stresses coordinated performance rather than the arms alone.

vocab.inContext: working through visible signals rather than electric transmission
a signal passed repeatedly from tower to tower
represented through agreed positions and their assigned meanings

skillTips.main-idea: State both the coordinated visual method and its weather-and-darkness limit; the history includes achievement and constraint.
skillTips.inference: Connect the telescope to the operator’s next action: copying an arm position displayed by the previous tower.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the repeated station-to-station copying to understand “relay” as passing a signal along a chain.
skillTips.detail: The demonstration year appears beside Chappe’s name in the opening paragraph, before the later network is described.

passages.title: The Communal Pantry of Acorn Woodpeckers
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An acorn woodpecker may return to a trunk dotted with hundreds of small holes. This is not random damage. In many groups, the birds use such a tree as a granary, fitting one acorn into each opening. The store is a shared resource rather than a private cupboard.

Group members gather acorns, drill holes, and guard the granary. As stored acorns dry, some shrink and loosen. The birds may move a loose acorn into a smaller hole, so maintaining the store continues after autumn gathering ends. One tree can be used over many years, with new holes added as older ones remain.

These woodpeckers also cooperate in raising young. Some group members help feed nestlings even when they are not the breeding parents. Their social life is complex, and not every population uses exactly the same storage pattern. In some parts of the species’ range, birds place acorns in natural cracks instead of drilling a central granary tree.

The familiar trunk therefore records repeated group labor. Its holes are not a plan drawn in advance by one bird. They accumulate through many trips, adjustments, and seasons. A durable common store emerges from small acts that different birds repeat and maintain.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Acorn woodpeckers use a new private storage tree during every season.
Every acorn woodpecker population drills one central tree in exactly the same way.
Groups of acorn woodpeckers build and maintain shared food stores through repeated labor, though their storage patterns can vary.
Acorn woodpeckers make trunk holes mainly to provide nests for unrelated birds.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes group gathering, guarding, and maintenance across years while noting that some populations use natural cracks instead.

questions.stem: Why can maintaining the granary continue after acorns have been stored?
choices: Every older hole disappears as soon as autumn ends.
Nestlings remove the acorns and replace them with insects.
The birds must turn each natural crack into a central tree.
Drying acorns may loosen, so birds need to refit them into smaller holes.
questions.explanation: The passage links drying with shrinking and loosening, then describes moving an acorn to a tighter hole.

questions.stem: What does “granary” mean in this passage?
choices: a shared place where food is stored
a nest used only by breeding parents
a random patch of damage in a trunk
a seasonal route between two forests
questions.explanation: The text immediately describes the granary as a tree where birds fit acorns into openings and share the stored resource.

questions.stem: What storage method do some populations use instead of a central granary tree?
choices: They bury every acorn beside a nest.
They place acorns in natural cracks.
They carry all stored food to another species.
They leave loose acorns on open branches.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that birds in some parts of the range use natural cracks rather than drilling a central granary.

lesson.strategy: Read the dotted trunk as a record of actions across time. Link gathering, refitting, guarding, and rearing young, while preserving the passage’s caution about population differences.

signals.means: This begins the cause-and-effect explanation for continued granary maintenance.
The passage expands group behavior from food storage to raising young.
The conclusion interprets the many holes as evidence of repeated shared labor.

vocab.inContext: a shared tree or place used to store acorns
young birds still being cared for in the nest
build up gradually through many repeated additions

skillTips.main-idea: Combine the shared work at the granary with the explicit limit that storage behavior varies across populations.
skillTips.inference: Follow the drying sequence: an acorn shrinks, its fit loosens, and a smaller hole restores a secure fit.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the phrases “fitting one acorn” and “shared resource” to define the function of a granary in context.
skillTips.detail: Look in the population-variation sentence for the alternative to drilling and maintaining one central tree.

passages.title: The Signs Before the Turn
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Good wayfinding begins before a person reaches the place where paths divide. A sign placed after the turn can confirm a choice, but it cannot help someone choose in time. Reliable routes therefore use a sequence: advance notice, direction at the decision point, and confirmation beyond it.

Words alone may not serve every traveler. A transit system can pair a station name with a number, color, or shape. A hospital can repeat the same floor symbol on a map, a wall, and a doorway. These cues are redundant, meaning that more than one feature carries the needed information. If a visitor misses one cue or cannot distinguish it easily, another may support the route.

Redundancy works only when the cues agree. A temporary arrow pointing left creates confusion if an uncovered permanent sign still points right. Small errors can also compound. Someone who makes one wrong turn may encounter signs intended for people arriving from another direction, making recovery harder.

For this reason, wayfinding is a system rather than a collection of labels. Designers must consider where decisions occur, what people can see from each approach, and how they can recover after an error. The strongest route is not the one with the most signs. It is the one whose few, consistent cues appear when they are needed and continue to confirm the traveler’s progress.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the passage’s main idea?
choices: Wayfinding succeeds whenever a route contains the greatest possible number of signs.
A single written label after each turn serves every traveler and prevents all mistakes.
Temporary arrows should remain visible beside permanent signs even when they disagree.
Reliable wayfinding uses timely, consistent, and redundant cues to guide choices and help travelers confirm or recover their routes.
questions.explanation: The passage combines sign timing, multiple forms of information, consistency, confirmation, and recovery into one route system.

questions.stem: Why may one wrong turn make later signs harder to use?
choices: The traveler may approach signs designed for people coming from a different direction.
Every sign disappears immediately after someone makes an error.
A wrong turn removes all station numbers and floor symbols.
Later signs always use more words than signs near the entrance.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says a mistaken traveler may meet signs meant for another approach, so those cues may not support recovery.

questions.stem: What does “redundant” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: placed only after a traveler has chosen a route
carrying the same needed information in more than one way
visible only to people who already know the building
made from temporary arrows that contradict permanent signs
questions.explanation: The passage defines redundant cues as multiple features, such as a name, number, color, or shape, carrying the needed information.

questions.stem: What three-part sequence does the passage recommend for a reliable route?
choices: A map, a worker, and a digital screen at the entrance
A station name, a hospital floor, and a doorway
Advance notice, direction at the decision point, and confirmation beyond it
A temporary arrow, a permanent arrow, and an uncovered label
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explicitly gives advance notice, clear direction at the choice, and confirmation after it as the sequence.

lesson.strategy: Map the route as three moments (before, at, and after a choice), then test every cue for redundancy and agreement. Use the wrong-turn example to add recovery to the system.

signals.means: This introduces the ordered placement of information along a reliable route.
The phrase limits redundancy: repeated information helps only when it is consistent.
The conclusion gathers timing, consistency, and recovery into a system view.

vocab.inContext: the system that helps people choose and confirm a route through a place
providing the needed information through more than one cue
grow into larger difficulties through added effects

skillTips.main-idea: Include cue timing, redundancy, consistency, and recovery; no single one captures the full wayfinding system.
skillTips.inference: Picture the wrong approach after a mistaken turn and ask which traveler the next set of signs was designed to guide.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the name-number-color-shape examples to see that “redundant” means repeating information through different features.
skillTips.detail: Retrieve the ordered three-part route from paragraph one and keep the moments before, at, and after the decision distinct.
